candidate.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care; recognize changes in condition, activate escalation systems, and coordinate timely evaluation
candidate.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — maternal early-warning trigger and escalation
candidate.educational_objective: Use maternal early-warning triggers to recognize possible deterioration and initiate timely protocol-based reassessment and escalation while continuing comprehensive clinical assessment.

options.A: Initiate the protocol-defined reassessment and escalation promptly because the trigger is designed to identify possible maternal deterioration before the exact diagnosis is known.
options.B: Use the trigger as proof of one specific diagnosis and begin diagnosis-specific treatment without further assessment.
options.C: Ignore the trigger if the client is postpartum because maternal early-warning systems apply only before delivery.
options.D: Stop performing broader clinical assessment because the warning score replaces bedside nursing judgment once a threshold is met.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. ACOG guidance describes maternal early-warning systems as a way to recognize physiologic changes or other triggers that may precede serious deterioration and require immediate further action according to protocol. A trigger is not itself a diagnosis; it prompts timely evaluation and escalation while the cause is determined. These systems are relevant to obstetric and postpartum emergencies and complement, rather than replace, clinical assessment. B overinterprets a screening trigger, C incorrectly excludes postpartum deterioration, and D abandons the bedside assessment the system is intended to support.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Maternal early-warning criteria are screening/escalation tools that identify possible clinical deterioration and trigger timely protocol-based evaluation; they are not stand-alone diagnoses and do not replace bedside assessment.
candidate.source_document_title: Preparing for Clinical Emergencies in Obstetrics and Gynecology
candidate.source_locator: Early Warning Systems in the Inpatient Setting — many emergencies are preceded by instability; triggers mandate further actions by the health care team according to protocol; bedside caregivers should recognize changes indicating an emergency requiring immediate intervention; each setting should define activation criteria

candidate.stem: A postpartum client develops a new abnormal vital-sign pattern that meets the hospital’s maternal early-warning trigger. Which nursing action best reflects the purpose of the early-warning system?
